opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the main reason is that the reasoning models were, in a sense, already priced in for me. If you'd asked me a couple of years earlier how we'd get from chatbots to systems that can do serious technical work, I would have said something like: you take a pretrained model, you let it think for longer, and you train it with reinforcement learning on tasks where you can check whether it got the answer right. That's roughly what o1 and o3 are. So when they arrived, my reaction was less "wow, this is a new paradigm I didn't see coming" and more "okay, this is the thing we expected, and it's working about as well as we'd hoped."

The way I think about timelines isn't "here's a specific technique and when it'll show up." It's more like a trend of steadily improving capabilities, driven by more compute, better algorithms, more data, and people finding new ways to use those things. Inference-time scaling and RL on verifiable tasks are exactly the kind of algorithmic progress that trend already assumes. If we had *never* found something like that, I'd have to update toward longer timelines. Finding it keeps us on trend rather than putting us ahead of it.

There's also a question about what the gains actually show. The jumps on math and competitive programming were very impressive, but those are domains where you can easily verify answers, which is exactly where you'd expect RL to shine. The harder question for timelines is how well that transfers to messy real-world work: long-horizon tasks, ambiguous goals, coordinating inside an organization, working out what problem to solve in the first place. I've seen some evidence of transfer, but not enough to make me think the hard parts are suddenly solved.

So it's a modest update, in the direction of "the trend is real and continuing," but not a big shift in my median. To be honest, my timelines were already fairly short, so it would take something quite surprising to move them much further in either direction.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that they didn't do much to change my timelines because they were roughly what I expected to happen. Not in the sense that I had predicted the specific form, like "someone is going to do RL on chain-of-thought and it's going to work really well on math and coding." But the thing I'd been expecting for a while was that there was a lot of low-hanging fruit in improving capabilities beyond just scaling pretraining, and that labs would find it. So when o1 came out, my reaction was more "okay, that's one of the things on the list" rather than "wow, the world is different now."

If you'd asked me a couple of years ago, I'd have said something like: pretraining scaling continues, but on top of that you get algorithmic improvements, better post-training, better use of inference-time compute, and these compound. Reasoning models are a pretty clean instance of the inference-time compute piece. It's a bit like the "test-time compute" story people had been talking about for a while, where you let the model think longer and you get better answers, and now you train it to be good at that. That was a thing I would have put reasonable probability on, so when it happened, the update is just "that probability went to one," which isn't a huge shift in the overall picture.

The other reason is that my timelines were already not that long. I've been saying for a while that I think there's a real chance of very capable, transformative systems within a decade, and when your distribution already has a lot of mass on the near term, individual pieces of evidence that are consistent with that don't move it much. You'd need something surprising in either direction. For example, if the reasoning approach had completely stalled out, or if it had worked great on math but then it turned out it just doesn't transfer at all to anything open-ended, that would have been an update towards longer. And conversely, if o3 had come out and been able to do, say, a week of autonomous research engineering with no human in the loop, that would have been an update towards shorter. Neither of those happened. What happened is impressive but in the expected range.

I'd also say I'm a bit wary of over-updating on benchmark results specifically. The benchmark jumps for o3 were very large, on things like ARC-AGI and FrontierMath, and those are genuinely hard tasks. But benchmarks are the thing labs optimize for, and historically the gap between "crushes the benchmark" and "can actually do the job" has been larger than people expect. So I try to think about what the models can do in the real world, and there the story is more continuous. People use them for coding, they're getting better at coding, the length of task they can do is going up. That's the trend I'm actually tracking, and reasoning models are on that trend rather than breaking it.

So, to sum up: it's not that I think reasoning models are unimportant. They're clearly a big deal for capabilities. It's that they were the kind of thing I already had priced in, and my timelines were already fairly short, so the net effect on my beliefs was small.

r001.rationale: The response says Shah anticipated capability gains from post-training and inference-time compute, but it explicitly says he had not predicted the specific use of RL on chain-of-thought. It does not clearly attribute his small timeline update to having anticipated RL’s role.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention AI debate or say its usefulness depends on reinforcement learning being used to build powerful AI systems.

r003.rationale: The response does not contrast the generalization of reinforcement learning in o1 and o3 with the generalization of instruction following.

r004.rationale: The response says the releases caused little change because they were expected, but does not say finer-grained tracking would probably have shifted Shah slightly toward longer timelines.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that they were broadly the sort of progress I was already expecting. I wasn’t imagining that we’d get to AGI solely by making pretraining runs bigger, while keeping everything else about how we build and use models fixed. My expectations already included finding better ways to train models to reason and giving them more computation to work through problems.

So o1 and o3 are evidence of progress, but you have to compare that progress to what you were forecasting. If you expected capabilities to stall, they should be a substantial update. If you expected continued rapid progress, seeing another substantial advance doesn’t necessarily move your timelines very much.

There’s also a gap between doing very well on tasks with clear, checkable answers and being able to reliably carry out the full range of work a human can do. These models tell us something about the former, but they don’t settle how quickly we’ll get the latter. So I’d update on the particular route we seem to be taking more than on the overall arrival date.

r001.rationale: The response says Shah expected better ways to train models to reason, but does not identify reinforcement learning as an anticipated route to powerful AI.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss AI debate or make its usefulness conditional on reinforcement learning.

r003.rationale: It contrasts checkable-answer tasks with the full range of human work, but does not compare reinforcement learning’s generalisation with instruction following’s.

r004.rationale: It says the advances would not necessarily move timelines much, but does not say finer-grained tracking would have shifted them slightly toward longer timelines.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that they were broadly consistent with what I was already expecting. I already expected that we’d find ways to get more useful work out of models by giving them more computation at inference time — letting them spend longer working through a problem rather than having to produce an answer immediately.

So the update isn’t, “These models are much better than the previous models, therefore my timelines should get much shorter.” It’s, “Are these models substantially better than I expected models to be at this point?” And for me, the answer was: not substantially enough to move things very much.

They’re an important advance. But if your existing forecast already includes important advances, seeing one happen doesn’t necessarily change the forecast.
